turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Before we get into it, the parking was a mess, we circled twice, and I almost had Denise drop me at the curb.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You made it, that's what counts. This was booked as a routine look at the blood pressure and the cholesterol medicine, yes?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, routine, though I've been turning the pills over in my head for weeks, Dr. Shah. I'm seventy-one in June, which is not why I came, I just keep announcing it.
[SEG0004] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I drove her. Frank, her husband, stayed home because his sugar's been up and down and he hates the waiting room.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright. How have you been feeling day to day?

[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Mostly okay, I think. I get tired, not sleepy-tired, more like the laundry basket feels heavier and I sit down in the middle of folding. I told myself it was just age, but it's been on my mind.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been talking about being tired since before Christmas. I hear it most Mondays when I come in.
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, I don't know about since Christmas. I'd say the last two months, after the weather turned and I stopped walking as much. Two months feels right to me.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): So somewhere between a couple of months and several. We'll leave the exact start loose. Anything else besides the tiredness?

[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): My calves cramp at night. Not every night, maybe three nights a week, both calves seize up and I have to stand on the cold bathroom floor until they let go. That's been years, really, even before the pill business.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Would you say those cramps are worse since you changed your medicines, or about the same?

[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose... sometimes, not really. Some weeks yes, then I'll go ten days with nothing and think I imagined it. I wouldn't want you to write down that they got worse.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair, I won't hang a change on that. Any chest pain?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None. I know that's the one you're supposed to speak up about, and I haven't had any.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Shortness of breath?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I can still get up the stairs, I just pause at the landing from the tired feeling, not because I can't breathe.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Dizziness, or lightheaded when you stand up?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No, not that. I stand up fine.
[SEG0019] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I haven't seen her grab for the wall or anything.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Tell me what you're actually taking. Start wherever you want.

[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): The blood pressure one I still take, for the high blood pressure I've had for years. Lisinopril, the little round one, ten milligrams. I don't take it every day anymore, I take it every other day, because I read it can be hard on the kidneys, and my pressure feels fine, so every other day seemed like splitting the difference.

[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm only there Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays. I set the lisinopril out those days, but she says she already took it, or that it's an off day, and I can't swear she's even doing every other day. Some weeks the bottle looks the same.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I am mostly doing every other day. I think. The week the grandkids came I lost track, so I won't promise it's perfect.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ten milligrams, aimed at every other day, and neither of you is sure it actually happens that way. What about the cholesterol tablet?

[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): I stopped it. Atorvastatin, the one for my high cholesterol. I was going to say forty milligrams, that's what I started on years ago, but no, you cut it to twenty, twenty milligrams, and I stopped after I read something online.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did you stop?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Spring. I want to say March, after this long article, but it might have been later. I didn't write it down, I just put the bottle in the back of the cabinet.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was still in the weekly box in April, I remember her birthday lunch, and then it wasn't. I can't give you a date either. Sometime in the spring.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): We don't need the exact day. What did you read?

[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): A health newsletter, then a Facebook thread, women my age saying statins ruined their muscles and their memory and their liver. One said her doctor never told her she could quit, and I know that isn't a journal, but I read the whole thing twice. My calves already cramp, so I thought, why am I swallowing something that might make that worse.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to scold you for reading. I do want this based on your numbers, not a comment thread. Did anyone ever tell you a result that worried you?

[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Last visit, or the one before, they said my cholesterol was borderline. They said the LDL was one-thirty something, I don't remember the exact figure, and they still wanted me on the pill. Borderline is the word that stuck, not a number I'd swear to.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She also got a phone call. She told me a nurse said a liver number was borderline, and that scared her more than Facebook, if you ask me.

[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, that call. They didn't say dangerous, they said borderline and we'd recheck, and then I don't think anybody rechecked it. Please don't write a number I can't remember, I don't have the paper.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): I won't invent a number. A prior cholesterol test and a liver test were both described as borderline, no exact values today. Any other medicines, aspirin?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Someone mentioned a baby aspirin once, years ago, and I never started it. I didn't even fill it. So that isn't one of mine.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): We won't count that. Allergies to medicines?
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of. Penicillin is fine, I've had it, no rashes or swelling.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Frank is the one with the diabetes pills. Metformin, a thousand milligrams twice a day, and Jardiance, I think. Separate blue case. She doesn't take those.

[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Absolutely not. He offered me a metformin after the church health fair, because they pricked my finger and said my sugar was a little high, no number, just a little high. I did not take his pill. I told him that was a ridiculous thing to offer your wife.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good that you didn't. His metformin and his Jardiance stay his. A fingerstick called a little high, with no number, is a vague old check, not a diagnosis.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): My mother had type two diabetes, in her sixties. My father had a heart attack at seventy-two. I figure that's why people fussed about my cholesterol in the first place.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): That family history matters. Do you smoke?

[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): Never. I tried one cigarette ages ago and hated it, so that doesn't count. I have one glass of wine with Frank on Saturdays, not a bottle, whatever he says when he's teasing.
[SEG0045] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She lives with Frank. I come three mornings a week, paid through the agency, meds and a meal and laundry. I'm not there nights.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check the pressure and look you over. Cuff on the right arm.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): That cuff always squeezes worse on the right. I remember that every visit and I still can't tell you why.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): 146 over 88. Pulse is 74. A bit higher than I'd like, which fits with the lisinopril not being daily, though one reading isn't the whole story.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heart sounds are regular, lungs are clear, and I don't see any swelling at the ankles.
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): I was going to say my shoes feel tight some evenings, but that's been forever and I don't think it's swelling. You just looked, so I'll drop it.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with urination, burning, going more often?
[SEG0052] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's all normal for me.
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stomach, bowels, heartburn?
[SEG0054] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I eat fine, too fine, honestly. Denise makes a very good soup and I never leave any.
[SEG0055] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Chicken and rice, yesterday. Not relevant, sorry.

[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thinking out loud. You stopped atorvastatin twenty milligrams, you're on lisinopril ten only every other day, and today is 146 over 88. My first instinct is to restart the statin at ten milligrams tonight, see you in six weeks, and do labs in three months. That would be the simple path.

[SEG0057] person_1 (PATIENT): If you want me to restart I will try, but that liver call is sitting in my head and I'd rather not swallow it tonight and worry. Also we're going to my son's in Ohio for about two weeks starting Friday. I can take pills along, I just don't want a brand new plan in his guest room.
[SEG0058] person_3 (CAREGIVER): If you're thinking of blood work in two weeks, she won't be here. I looked at the calendar this morning.

[SEG0059] person_2 (DOCTOR): That changes it. I'm not restarting the atorvastatin today. The borderline liver comment, even without a number, plus you being away, means I want fresh labs before we decide. Scratch the ten milligram restart, and scratch the six-week visit.
[SEG0060] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. I appreciate you not making me feel foolish. I really did read that article like it was homework, which is embarrassing to say out loud.

[SEG0061] person_2 (DOCTOR): Here's the plan I'm actually going with. I'll put the orders in now, a lipid panel and a comprehensive metabolic panel, kidneys because of the lisinopril and liver because of that old comment. This week if they can take you tomorrow morning, or the day you get back, but it's ordered either way.
[SEG0062] person_1 (PATIENT): Tomorrow morning? I can skip breakfast. I always think these must be fasting and then someone says half of them aren't, and I overthink the slip every time.
[SEG0063] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fasting helps the lipid panel, water is fine. Front desk can book the draw, and the orders stand either way.
[SEG0064] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get her there tomorrow if they'll take her. Morning's free.

[SEG0065] person_2 (DOCTOR): On the lisinopril, I'd like you back to every day, ten milligrams, not every other day. If you get dizzy or faint, hold it and call, but I don't want the every-other-day plan continued.
[SEG0066] person_1 (PATIENT): Every day. I can do that. I made the every-other-day thing up myself, nobody told me to, and I'll start tonight, which would have been an on day anyway.
[SEG0067] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't take any of Frank's diabetes pills, even if some fingerstick again says a little high. That isn't how we treat you.
[SEG0068] person_1 (PATIENT): I won't. I only brought it up so you'd know he offered, not that I took one.

[SEG0069] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll revisit the statin decision in a month, once you're back and the labs are in. That visit is a plan, not a maybe. If the numbers look safe we can talk about restarting then, maybe at ten, maybe staying off, and I am not deciding that today.
[SEG0070] person_1 (PATIENT): A month. I can put that on the fridge. Should I worry the tiredness is my heart? That's where my mind goes at two in the morning.

[SEG0071] person_2 (DOCTOR): I don't have a reason to call this a heart problem today. My working impression is the tiredness and the night cramps are there, the pressure is a little high off daily lisinopril, and you've got the longstanding high blood pressure and the cholesterol issue with the statin on hold until labs. Provisional, not a final diagnosis.

[SEG0072] person_1 (PATIENT): The cramps might just be my cramps, because I still have them off the pill. I've been off it for months and they didn't vanish, which I suppose is information. I'm talking in a circle, sorry.

[SEG0073] person_2 (DOCTOR): It cuts against the statin being the only cause. It isn't proof. If you get chest pain, pressure, or real shortness of breath, don't wait the month, call 911 or go to the ER.
[SEG0074] person_1 (PATIENT): I understand. Denise will remember that better than I will.
[SEG0075] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll write it next to the lab and the one-month visit. Chest pain means the ER, not a phone message.
[SEG0076] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything from the drugstore, ibuprofen, supplements?
[SEG0077] person_1 (PATIENT): A multivitamin sometimes, not every day, I forget. No ibuprofen. The vitamin is huge, so sometimes, not really a routine.
[SEG0078] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then I won't list a vitamin as a regular medicine. You started to say the article mentioned diabetes.

[SEG0079] person_1 (PATIENT): It said statins cause diabetes. With my mother, and that health-fair prick, I spiraled, and I almost bought a glucose monitor and then didn't. So I have worry, not home numbers.

[SEG0080] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not adding a diabetes diagnosis off a little-high fingerstick and family history. I thought about ordering an A1c today, and I'm not. The metabolic panel shows a glucose, and an A1c can wait if we need it. One plan, not three.
[SEG0081] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She'll ask me tomorrow if you ordered the A1c. I'll tell her no.
[SEG0082] person_2 (DOCTOR): Correct, not today. Lipid panel and comprehensive metabolic panel only.
[SEG0083] person_1 (PATIENT): And the statin stays in the cabinet. I won't restart it on my own just because I feel guilty in Ohio.
[SEG0084] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't. We look at the results together in a month and decide then. Lisinopril every day, ten milligrams, and call if you feel faint on it.
[SEG0085] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright. Thank you for not lecturing me. I'll try to stop treating Facebook like a second opinion. Not promising I'll succeed.
[SEG0086] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll have her at the lab in the morning, and the one-month visit goes on the fridge when we have a time.
[SEG0087] person_2 (DOCTOR): Reception will hand you the lab slip and a follow-up card on the way out. We're done for today.

spec.situation: Patient on routine review who admits stopping the cholesterol tablet after reading something online, still takes the BP tablet but 'every other day'; mentions husband's diabetes pills; doctor does not scold, plans repeat blood tests and revisits the statin decision in a month.
features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

omissions.text: Atorvastatin stop timing was sometime in the spring, likely around March or later, not exactly known.

Patient stopped atorvastatin after reading online concerns about muscle problems, memory problems, liver effects, and diabetes; she was also frightened by a prior phone call saying a liver test was 'borderline'.
Prior cholesterol result was described as 'borderline' with LDL remembered only as 'one-thirty something'; no exact value available.
Patient specifically reported no medication allergies and stated she has tolerated penicillin without rash or swelling.
Patient denied ever starting baby aspirin despite it being mentioned years ago.
Patient denied taking her husband's metformin or Jardiance after a church health fair fingerstick was said to be 'a little high'.
Fingerstick glucose was from a church health fair and was only described as 'a little high' with no number; doctor said this was not a diagnosis of diabetes.
Doctor noted the blood pressure reading was taken with the cuff on the right arm.
Patient reported pausing at the stair landing because of tiredness, not because of breathlessness.
Patient reported no lightheadedness on standing and said she stands up fine.
Patient mentioned shoes can feel tight in the evenings but said this has been longstanding and doctor found no ankle swelling.
Doctor's initial plan to restart atorvastatin at 10 mg tonight, see her in six weeks, and do labs in three months was explicitly changed and cancelled.
Current statin plan is specifically not to restart atorvastatin today because of the prior borderline liver comment and upcoming travel; decision deferred until after fresh labs.
Labs were to be done this week if possible, ideally tomorrow morning, or otherwise the day she returns from travel.
Patient will be away for about two weeks starting Friday, which affected timing of labs and follow-up planning.

Doctor advised that if she gets dizzy or faint on daily lisinopril, she should hold it and call; patient acknowledged the every-other-day regimen was self-devised and would restart daily dosing that night.
Doctor gave red-flag advice for 'chest pain, pressure, or real shortness of breath' specifically to call 911 or go to the ER rather than wait a month.
Patient takes a multivitamin only sometimes and not as a regular medication; no ibuprofen use.
Doctor considered ordering an A1c but explicitly decided not to order it today; only lipid panel and comprehensive metabolic panel were ordered.

clinical_uncertainties.description: The patient said the tiredness has lasted about two months, while the caregiver said it has been present since before Christmas, and no single duration was agreed.
No one can date when atorvastatin was stopped, only that it was sometime in the spring.
She aims to take lisinopril every other day, but she loses track and the caregiver cannot confirm the bottle is used that way, so actual adherence is unknown.

contradictions_detected: Duration of tiredness disagrees: patient reports about two months, caregiver reports since before Christmas.
ambiguous_entities: Whether calf cramps worsened after stopping the statin was answered 'mm, I suppose, sometimes, not really' and is not recorded as a change.
Evening shoe tightness was mentioned and then withdrawn, and is not recorded as swelling.
Multivitamin use was 'sometimes, not really a routine' and is not recorded as a medicine.
Recalled LDL was only 'one-thirty something', and the cholesterol test, liver test, and fingerstick were only called borderline or a little high, so no numeric results were recorded.

bad.reason: Current tiredness supported, but duration uncertain; exact '2 months to several months' wasn't stated by patient.
bad.text: tiredness (category=constitutional, status=present, duration=approximately 2 months to several months, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Atorvastatin stop date was sometime in the spring, possibly March or later, and the patient had started at 40 mg years ago before it was reduced to 20 mg.
Patient specifically denied any known medication allergy and stated penicillin is tolerated without rash or swelling.
The blood pressure reading was taken with the cuff on the right arm.
